title: Perceptions about fake news in Portuguese higher education students: An analysis of consumption and attitudes
screen_reason: Online survey of 602 Portuguese higher-education students aged 17-25 (April-May 2018) about their contact with fake news. Section 8.3 reports a self-reported encounter share with an explicit denominator: 56% of the sample say they have been deceived by fake news ('Un poco mas de la mitad (56%) de la muestra afirma haber sido enganados por noticias falsas'), with a recency breakdown (73.1% of those episodes in the past year). That is a RECALL estimate (self-reported contact with misinformation). It is borderline because the numerator is 'was deceived by', which is stricter than 'came across' and imports a belief component; it is a lower bound on encounter. All other numbers in the paper are awareness, attitude, definition or channel-distribution items.

estimates.platform: Online questionnaire distributed by e-mail through lecturers at ten Portuguese higher-education institutions
estimates.measure_type: % of student respondents who say they have been deceived by fake news
estimates.value_raw: 56% of the 602-respondent sample ('Un poco mas de la mitad (56%) de la muestra'); of those episodes, 73.1% occurred in the past year, 20.7% two or three years ago, 6.3% more than three years ago
estimates.denominator: 602 higher-education students in Portugal aged 17-25 (23.4% men, 76.6% women; 33.9% aged 17-20, 66.1% aged 21-25; 97.5% habitual social media users)
estimates.definition: Respondent affirms having been deceived by fake news at some point (no fixed window; the follow-up item places 73.1% of these episodes in the last year)
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper adopts no single definition but frames fake news as a piece that combines three features: "elementos esteticos similares a los de la informacion periodistica; adopcion de formatos narrativos propios del periodismo; intencionalidad desinformativa" [aesthetic elements similar to journalistic information; adoption of journalistic narrative formats; disinformative intent] (Romero-Rodriguez, Valle-Razo & Torres-Toukoumidis 2018), alongside Allcott & Gentzkow's 'intentionally and knowingly false news pieces that can mislead readers'. Crucially, respondents were NOT given a definition before answering - the questionnaire measured what they themselves understand by the term.
estimates.source_quote: Un poco más de la mitad (56%) de la muestra afirma haber sido engañados por noticias falsas, lo que sucedió en el últi- mo año el 73,1% de las veces; hace dos o tres años (20,7%); y hace más de tres años (6,3%).
estimates.page_loc: Section 8.3 'Percepcion y actitudes con respecto a las noticias falsas', p. 9
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Entirely self-reported; no verification of anything the respondents encountered. The paper's own central finding is that respondents' conceptions of 'fake news' diverge and are sometimes wrong: in a multiple-response item, 97% counted 'deliberately false news disguised as true news', 73% counted 'false information inadvertently shared by citizens on the internet' and a clickbait headline, 38% counted 'news with a sensationalist angle', 27% 'news with superficial treatment of the subject', 21% 'news with apparently unintentional inaccuracies by the journalist' and 20% 'news in which the ideological view is heavily emphasised'. The 56% therefore aggregates heterogeneous personal definitions.
estimates.moderator_quote: La muestra se ha recogido recurriendo a una metodologia no probabilistica y por conveniencia. El cuestionario, presentado en una plataforma online, fue divulgado mediante correo electronico por docentes de ensenanza superior de diferentes disciplinas cientificas en diez instituciones portuguesas, quienes los hicieron llegar a los estudiantes durante los meses de abril y mayo de 2018. [The sample was collected using a non-probabilistic convenience methodology. The online questionnaire was circulated by e-mail by lecturers from different disciplines at ten Portuguese institutions, who passed it to students during April and May 2018.]
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE, flagged for adjudication. The numerator is 'haber sido enganados por' - having been DECEIVED by fake news - not merely having seen it. Being deceived entails having encountered it, so 56% is a valid but conservative encounter estimate; a reviewer who reads the instruction 'Belief in false claims does NOT count' strictly could argue this measures deception (belief) rather than exposure and drop it. I kept it because it is a self-reported personal encounter experience, not an accuracy-judgement task on claims supplied by the researchers. Two further cautions: (1) no time window is attached to the 56% (the recency item is asked only of those who said yes, and 56% x 73.1% would be a computed product barred by R8, so no past-year figure is extractable); (2) respondents supplied their own definition of fake news, which the paper shows to be broad and inconsistent (38% count sensationalism, 27% superficial treatment) - hence breadth=misleading rather than false. Convenience sample of students from ten institutions, 76.6% female, so population_scope=other, not general_public. Article written in Spanish about a Portuguese sample. source_quote is the exact Spanish span from the text file (the hyphen-space in 'el ulti- mo ano' is the printed line break); other quoted fields are ASCII-transliterated with English translations in brackets. Translation of source_quote: 'A little more than half (56%) of the sample say they have been deceived by fake news, which happened in the last year in 73.1% of cases; two or three years ago (20.7%); and more than three years ago (6.3%).'

missed_or_uncertain: (a) '98,3% de los participantes ya habia oido hablar' [98.3% had already heard of fake news] - awareness that the phenomenon exists, NOT an encounter with it; deliberately not extracted, and it should not be read as a 98.3% exposure rate. (b) The channel distribution for the last fake news encountered (49% news shared by friends on social networks, 32% shared directly by news media on social networks, 11% on a news outlet's website, 7% offline) sums to 99% of 'los encuestados', which implies almost the whole sample had encountered fake news, but the paper never states an encounter share, so nothing is extractable - and the implied ~99% sits oddly against the 56% deceived figure, suggesting the channel item was asked only of those who reported an encounter. This inconsistency is the main reason confidence is medium. (c) 59.6% said they had doubts and sought clarification about the last fake news they saw, 22.5% came across contrary information by chance, 17.8% were actively alerted by someone - a distribution over how the deception was detected, not a prevalence. (d) 91.8% consider fake news a worrying phenomenon; 99.3% think fake news can influence opinion formation; 82.3% report a behaviour change - attitudes. (e) Definition items (97%, 73%, 38%, 27%, 21%, 20% etc.) measure what respondents think fake news IS, not what they met. (f) Media-use and news-consumption shares (97.5% social media users, 75% news on websites, 63% on social networks, 71% Instagram, 68% Facebook/YouTube, 16% Twitter) carry no veracity component. (g) 'solo el 16% de los jovenes' and the '17% of US citizens' figure in the discussion are cited from other sources - barred by R8.

rob.design: Exploratory descriptive cross-sectional online survey, 22 questions, piloted on five people. Eligibility: enrolled higher-education student in Portugal, any cycle, discipline or location, aged 17-25. NON-PROBABILISTIC CONVENIENCE sample: the online questionnaire was e-mailed by lecturers in different disciplines at ten Portuguese institutions to their students during April and May 2018; no sampling frame, no response rate, and no denominator of invitees is reported, so self-selection cannot be assessed. Realised sample n = 602, heavily female (76.6%) and skewed to social sciences (47.7%) and humanities (27%). All measures self-reported; no verification of any encountered item. Key instrument weakness for prevalence purposes: respondents were not given a definition of fake news before reporting their contact with it, and the paper's own results show their working definitions diverge widely (from deliberate fabrication to sensationalist or superficial reporting), so the numerator's construct is set by each respondent. Item non-response is substantial where it can be checked: of the 56% who said they had been deceived, only 36% (n = 152) answered the open question describing the last fake news item. Analysis is descriptive percentages only; no significance testing, weighting or CIs.

[a fake news item is a piece that generally brings together three characteristics: aesthetic elements similar to those of journalistic information; adoption of journalistic narrative formats; disinformative intent.]
